article.title: Van Hollen as Majority Leader
article.author: Richard W. Behan
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Big shoutout for the blue tsunami. Sooner than we dared dream MAGA is dangling from the ropes. When the Democratic Congress convenes next January we can reasonably expect reversals of Trump’s most heinous policies: the Iran war, the tariffs, the drastic cuts in healthcare and nutrition benefits. Jeffries in the House, and both Schumer and Van Hollen in the Senate seem willing and able to advance this agenda; all three have verbalized most of it. Reclaiming a pre-Trump status quo seems a Congressional shoo-in, and if Trump vetos the reform measures he’ll be orchestrating a total collapse of the Republican Party in 2028. MAGA will be a memory, but MAGA is not our most urgent political problem. Long before Trump’s caustic presidencies corporate oligarchy took command of federal governance, tilting public policy routinely to favor corporate interests over the wellbeing of the nation. Senator Van Hollen knows this He rages against “...rigging the government in favor of billionaires and corporations while leaving the rest of us to pay the price.” (See his website .) Senator Schumer, on the other hand, is part of the problem. Over the years he has taken more than $19 million in campaign contributions from corporate sources, notably from the Wall Street banks. He is supported handsomely by AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups. Related: No Kings? SCOTUS Has Been a Workable Stand-In for 223 Years As an agent of corporate oligarchy Schumer is not the person to challenge it. We need Van Hollen. Tackling corporate oligarchy, regaining a functioning democracy, calls for his independent, bold, and determined effort. Democracy in America was sabotaged—corporate oligarchy germinated—about thirty years ago. Arandom convergence occurred, of several absurd Supreme Court decisions, Ronald Reagan’s misbegotten presidency, and two world-class hypocrites, Bill and Hillary Clinton. In the late 1800’s the Supreme Court declared U.S. corporations to be legal persons, with rights guaranteed by the Constitution, including the freedom of speech and the right “to petition government for a redress of grievances.” A century later the Court said spending money in political campaigns is a form of free speech and therefor could not be abridged. And lobbying could not be abridged, either: the right of petition guarantees that. Corporations were empowered to donate as much and lobby as much as they pleased, potentially to dominate the crafting of public policy. Only one brute fact prevented them from overcoming democracy altogether. Until late in the 20 th century. corporations were numerous, typically small, and in fierce competition with others. They simply could not afford to lavish money on office seekers, or to hire expensive lobbyists. Enter Ronald Reagan in 1981, whose presidency was guided not by the problems and opportunities facing the nation, but by his obsession with neoliberal ideology. Government is the problem, he said, stifling free enterprise with burdensome regulations. For most of the 20 th century, for example, American corporations had been stifled by anit-trust laws, preventing them from growing into the savage behemoths of the Gilded Age. That’s why they were small, competitive, and cash-strapped. Reagan suspended enforcement of those laws. Thus unstifled American corporations, through mergers and acquisitions, plummeted in number and exploded in size. Some 3,908 corporations are traded on the stock exchanges these days, almost exactly half the high-water mark of 8,090 in the last century. Most of them in fact pose no threat to democracy, but the largest of them do: the top 500 American corporations account for 91.2% of the total of U.S. market capitalization. Here we’ll find the corporate oligarchs. Reagan’s dogmatism drove virtually every industry in the country into textbook oligopoly—a few giant corporations in control, largely escaping the constraints of competitive pricing. Today ten gigantic combines of supermarket chains sell more than 90% of the all the groceries bought nationwide. This condition holds for nearly every other item of consumer goods, from books to power tools. Diminished competition inevitably raises prices; in the U.S. today, according to economist Thomas Phillipon, living costs for American families have escalated by about $5,000 per year. Ronald Reagan is responsible for the affordability crisis raging today, not Donald Trump. Trump merely exacerbates it. Related: The Peril of Spectacle, Especially Jeffrey Epstein’s Next came the Clintons. Over the course of their four presidential campaigns, Bill and Hillary Clinton claimed to be the champions of working class Americans. But during those years they accepted from Wall Street banks a total of $93 million . In exchange they destroyed the Democratic Party’s historic affiliation with American labor. It began in 1992. Bill Clinton, taking a cue from Republican candidates, enlisted corporate sources for much of his campaign funding. In office he rewarded his benefactors by moving the Democratic Party sharply rightward: “The era of big government is over,” he announced, and then took action to “...end welfare as we know it.” In Clinton’s preferred term the New Democratic Party joined the Republicans in accommodating, even welcoming corporate oligarchy. Chris Van Hollen at the time was serving in the Maryland legislature. He sponsored the Maryland Fair Campaign Finance Act, previewing his concern with the issue today. The next president George W. Bush embraced corporate oligarchy, taking us into a fraudulent "war on terrorism." In fact a war for oil and empire, the American people paid in blood and taxes while the nation’s corporations prospered. The grip of corporate oligarchy was tightening, and then in 2010 the Supreme Court decided Citizens United. The guard rails vanished. The millions in corporate campaign finance surged into the billions.Senator Van Hollen watched as the peril grew, and in 2019 he introduced a Constitutional amemdment to overturn Citizens. “It’s time we finally end the outside influence of special interest spending that is corrupting our democracy,” he said at the time. Corporate oligarchy prevailed. In the 2024 presidential campaign, small individual contributions ($200 or less) amounted to 16% of the total. That could be called the American people’s effort. “Business” donations, according to the Open Secrets organization, totaled 60.4%. And corporate lobbying? Corporations outspend citizen groups by a factor of 86:1. The American people are stratospherically outgunned. Democracy was defeated long before Trump’s autocracy: his Administration is merely corporate oligarchy on steroids. Defeating MAGA will strip away its steroids, but not corporate oligarchy’s hammerlock. Chris Van Hollen as Majority Leader will be a potent adversary. Note: this article was drawn from a book the author is completing, The Triumph of Corporate Oligarchy: How It Defeated Democracy, Ravaged a Thriving Nation, Normalized Fraudulent Warfare, and Brought Forth Donald Trump
